metadata.summary: These Canadian recommendations address ophthalmic screening and monitoring for children and adolescents with juvenile idiopathic arthritis, alongside treatment of associated uveitis. They cover topical and systemic treatment decisions, treatment escalation, and care for acute anterior uveitis in children and adolescents with spondyloarthritis. The recommendations adapt earlier guidance to Canadian considerations of access, cost, and equity.

care_settings: Eye care in rural and remote areas
target_population: Children and adolescents with JIA-associated uveitis
therapeutic_areas: Education about warning signs of acute anterior uveitis

toxicities.event: Ocular complications associated with prolonged topical GC use

management.severity: CAU requiring more than 2 drops per day of prednisolone acetate 1% (or equivalent) at 3 months after the start of uveitis treatment, without systemic therapy
management.actions: Conditionally recommend adding systemic therapy to enable tapering of topical GCs rather than continuing topical GCs alone.

management.severity: CAU requiring more than 2 drops per day of prednisolone acetate 1% (or equivalent) for at least 3 months while receiving systemic therapy for uveitis control
management.actions: Conditionally recommend changing or escalating systemic therapy rather than maintaining the current systemic treatment.

prevention: Avoid prolonged topical GC use to reduce the risk of increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation.

When CAU is controlled with systemic therapy but still requires 1-2 drops/day of prednisolone acetate 1% (or equivalent), the guideline strongly recommends tapering topical GCs before tapering systemic therapy.

conditions.name: juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA)
conditions.description: Children and adolescents with JIA require assessment for uveitis, which may initially cause no symptoms.
conditions.epidemiology: The cumulative incidence of new-onset uveitis during the first 5 years after JIA diagnosis was 13.9%.

subtypes.name: oligoarthritis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: One of the JIA subtypes included in the guideline's high-risk group for uveitis when the other specified risk criteria are also met.

subtypes.name: polyarthritis (rheumatoid factor negative)
subtypes.distinguishing_features: One of the JIA subtypes included in the guideline's high-risk group for uveitis when the other specified risk criteria are also met.

subtypes.name: psoriatic arthritis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: One of the JIA subtypes included in the guideline's high-risk group for uveitis when the other specified risk criteria are also met.

subtypes.name: undifferentiated arthritis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: One of the JIA subtypes included in the guideline's high-risk group for uveitis when the other specified risk criteria are also met.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify a risk factor for JIA-associated uveitis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A positive result contributes to the specified high-risk profile together with an eligible JIA subtype, age < 7 years at JIA onset, and JIA duration of ≤ 4 years.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect ocular inflammation that may be asymptomatic.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After JIA diagnosis and regularly thereafter; for newly diagnosed asymptomatic patients, the first examination should occur as early as possible, within the first 1 to 3 months.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An ophthalmologist is preferred for screening. Another eyecare provider may perform it when timely access is otherwise unavailable, with subsequent verification by an ophthalmologist with uveitis expertise when possible.

follow_up.schedule: For children and adolescents at high risk of CAU, ophthalmic screening is conditionally recommended at least every 3 months for the first 4 years of disease. Newly diagnosed asymptomatic patients should receive an initial examination as early as possible, within the first 1 to 3 months.
long_term_effects: JIA-associated uveitis can cause permanent vision loss.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline emphasizes coordination between rheumatology and ophthalmology and informing caregivers about the importance of timely screening despite the absence of ocular symptoms.

conditions.name: chronic anterior uveitis (CAU)
conditions.description: CAU associated with JIA can threaten vision. Ocular inflammation may remain controlled only while topical steroids are continued; the guideline includes such steroid-dependent disease within active uveitis.
conditions.epidemiology: Chronic, asymptomatic anterior uveitis occurs in up to 20% of children with JIA.
conditions.clinical_presentation: CAU may be asymptomatic. Posterior synechiae or cataracts can occur as complications of uveitis and indicate a poor visual outcome.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Detect and monitor ocular inflammation, disease control, and complications.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During screening and ongoing monitoring of JIA-associated CAU.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline defines new CAU activity as either first-onset uveitis or loss of control of previously controlled uveitis.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate loss of efficacy over time during biologic treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The cited SHARE group advises considering testing if efficacy declines over time.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline reports no direct evidence in uveitis establishing the effect of antidrug antibodies on biologic efficacy.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate loss of efficacy over time during biologic treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: The cited SHARE group advises considering testing if efficacy declines over time.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The guideline reports no direct evidence in uveitis establishing the effect of low trough levels on biologic efficacy.

follow_up.schedule: For controlled uveitis, ophthalmic monitoring is strongly recommended within 1 month after each reduction or discontinuation change to topical GC, no less frequently than every 3 months on stable therapy, and within 2 months after a change made to taper or discontinue systemic therapy. The group also agreed on a maximum 3-month interval for monitoring uveitis when considering whether to add systemic therapy.
long_term_effects: Uveitis can result in permanent vision loss.
Posterior synechiae and cataracts associated with uveitis indicate a poor visual outcome.
Prolonged topical GC use can increase intraocular pressure and cause cataracts.
follow_up.survivorship_notes: Ongoing care requires coordination between rheumatology and ophthalmology; treatment may entail frequent visits and adjustments.

conditions.name: acute anterior uveitis
conditions.description: The guideline addresses education about AAU warning signs in children and adolescents with SpA and treatment of an isolated, short-lived episode in patients whose disease is otherwise well controlled with systemic immunosuppressive therapy.

conditions.name: SpA
conditions.description: The guideline addresses children and adolescents with SpA in relation to recognition and treatment of AAU.

follow_up.survivorship_notes: The guideline strongly recommends education about AAU warning signs to reduce delays in treatment, symptom duration, or uveitis complications.

therapies_index.name: prednisolone acetate 1%
therapies_index.administration: Topical eye drops. The guideline uses a requirement for more than 2 drops per day at 3 months after treatment begins, or for at least 3 months during systemic therapy, as a threshold for considering a change in treatment.
key_toxicities: Prolonged topical GC use may increase intraocular pressure and cause cataracts.
Evidence cited in the guideline associates more than 2 topical GC drops per day with ocular complications.
monitoring: When topical GC is reduced or stopped in controlled uveitis, an eye examination is recommended within 1 month of each change.

therapies_index.name: difluprednate
key_toxicities: The guideline identifies increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation as potential effects of prolonged topical GC use.
monitoring: When topical GC is reduced or stopped in controlled uveitis, an eye examination is recommended within 1 month of each change.

therapies_index.name: topical GCs
therapies_index.administration: Eye drops are used for short-term control of active CAU and as initial treatment for an isolated, short-lived episode of AAU.
key_toxicities: Prolonged use can increase intraocular pressure and cause cataracts.
The cited evidence reports a risk of ocular complications with more than 2 drops per day; the working group considered the risk higher with long-term use of 3 or more drops per day.
monitoring: Consider adding systemic therapy by a maximum 3-month monitoring interval when topical drops remain necessary for uveitis control.
In controlled uveitis, arrange ophthalmic monitoring within 1 month after each topical GC reduction or discontinuation.

therapies_index.name: MTX
therapies_index.administration: Retrospective studies cited doses of 15 mg/m2 (alternatively up to 1 mg/kg) to a maximum of 25 mg weekly. Both subcutaneous and oral administration are discussed; the guideline does not prefer one route over the other.
monitoring: For well-controlled uveitis, ophthalmic monitoring is recommended within 2 months of a systemic therapy change.

therapies_index.name: adalimumab (ADA)
therapies_index.administration: The product-monograph regimen described is 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks for patients weighing more than 30 kg. The guideline also describes treatment with 40 mg subcutaneously weekly to pursue maximal clinical benefit.

therapies_index.name: infliximab
therapies_index.administration: The guideline states that shortening the interval to less than every 4 weeks and/or raising the dose to more than 10 mg/kg can be considered.

therapies_index.name: monoclonal antibody TNFi
therapies_index.administration: If response at standard JIA dosing is inadequate, the guideline conditionally favors optimizing the current agent’s dose and/or frequency before changing to another monoclonal antibody TNFi.
monitoring: For loss of efficacy over time, recommendations from the cited SHARE group suggest considering antidrug antibody and drug trough-level testing; the guideline notes that direct evidence for their effect on efficacy in uveitis is absent.

therapies_index.name: ADA biosimilars
approved_indications: Pediatric uveitis: the guideline reports Health Canada indications for 4 new ADA biosimilars as of May 2021.

special_populations.population: Patients living in rural or remote areas
special_populations.considerations: Travel and limited local access to eye care may make timely screening difficult. Some patients live more than 2000 km from their treating center.
The document identifies federally regulated coverage through the Non-Insured Health Benefits program as a consideration when assessing access to care.

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA at high risk of CAU, perform ophthalmic screening at least every 3 months for at least the first 4 years of disease rather than using another screening frequency. For newly diagnosed patients without symptoms, arrange the initial examination as early as possible, within the first 1 to 3 months after diagnosis.
recommendations.context: High risk includes oligoarthritis, polyarthritis (rheumatoid factor negative), psoriatic arthritis, or undifferentiated arthritis together with antinuclear antibody positivity, age < 7 years at JIA onset, and JIA duration of ≤ 4 years.
recommendations.rationale: CAU can be asymptomatic, so delayed initial or repeated screening can delay its detection. Screening frequency reflects the risk of developing uveitis during the early years of JIA.

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and controlled uveitis who are tapering or stopping topical GC, conduct ophthalmic monitoring within 1 month after each topical GC change rather than monitoring less often.
recommendations.context: Controlled uveitis during a topical GC change.

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and controlled uveitis receiving stable therapy, perform ophthalmic monitoring at least every 3 months rather than less frequently.

For children and adolescents with JIA and controlled uveitis who are tapering or stopping systemic therapy, conduct ophthalmic monitoring within 2 months of the systemic therapy change rather than monitoring less often.
recommendations.context: Controlled uveitis during a systemic therapy change.

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU, favor PSL acetate 1% topical drops over difluprednate topical drops.
recommendations.context: Choice of topical GC for active CAU.

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU, add or increase topical GCs for short-term control rather than adding systemic GCs.

For children and adolescents with JIA and CAU who still require more than 2 drops per day of prednisolone acetate 1% or equivalent at 3 months after starting uveitis treatment and are not receiving systemic therapy, add systemic therapy to permit tapering of topical GCs rather than continuing topical GCs alone.
recommendations.context: Persistent topical GC requirement without systemic therapy.
recommendations.rationale: Published data indicate a risk of ocular complications with more than 2 topical GC drops per day; prolonged use of 3 or more drops per day raises concern about treatment-related complications.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Recommendations 2 and 3; Table 2, GC use

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and CAU who have needed more than 2 drops per day of prednisolone acetate 1% or equivalent for at least 3 months despite receiving systemic therapy for uveitis, change or escalate systemic therapy rather than maintain the current systemic treatment.
recommendations.context: Persistent topical GC requirement while receiving systemic therapy.
recommendations.rationale: The working group identified an increased risk of complications with prolonged use of 3 or more topical GC drops per day.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Recommendations 2 and 3; Table 2, GC use

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA who develop new CAU activity despite stable systemic therapy, use topical GCs before changing or escalating systemic therapy rather than changing or escalating systemic treatment immediately.
recommendations.context: New activity means either uveitis without a prior episode or loss of control of previously controlled uveitis.

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and CAU beginning systemic treatment for CAU, use methotrexate (MTX) as the first-line DMARD.
recommendations.rationale: Retrospective studies and subsequent systematic reviews support MTX treatment; despite the generally limited study quality, its evidence base is more substantial than that of the other conventional DMARDs discussed.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Recommendation 4; Table 2, DMARDs and biologics

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU starting a TNFi, choose a monoclonal antibody TNFi rather than ETN.
recommendations.context: Initial TNFi selection for active CAU.

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU whose response to one monoclonal antibody TNFi at standard JIA dosing is inadequate, optimize the dose and/or administration frequency of that TNFi rather than switch to another monoclonal antibody TNFi.
recommendations.context: Inadequate response to the current monoclonal antibody TNFi.
recommendations.rationale: Randomized controlled trials directly comparing monoclonal TNFis for JIA-associated CAU are unavailable. Patient/caregiver advisors preferred adjusting a current regimen over introducing another medication unless a clear benefit justified the change.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Recommendation 5; Table 2, DMARDs and biologics

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU who have not responded to a first monoclonal antibody TNFi given at above standard dose and/or frequency, switch to another monoclonal antibody TNFi rather than a biologic from a different class.
recommendations.context: Failure of the first monoclonal antibody TNFi after dose and/or frequency escalation.

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU who have failed MTX and 2 monoclonal antibody TNFis at optimized doses, favor abatacept (ABA) or tocilizumab (TCZ) as bDMARD options over the nbDMARD options MMF, leflunomide, or cyclosporine.
recommendations.context: CAU refractory to MTX and 2 optimized monoclonal antibody TNFis.
recommendations.rationale: Direct evidence to guide treatment after failure of 2 monoclonal TNFis is unavailable; the preference reflects working-group expert opinion informed by observational data.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Recommendation 6; Table 2, DMARDs and biologics

recommendations.statement: Educate children and adolescents with SpA about the warning signs of AAU to reduce delays in treatment, symptom duration, or uveitis complications.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Table 2, Education about treatment of AAU

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with SpA whose disease is well controlled with systemic immunosuppressive therapy and who experience an isolated, short-lived AAU episode, do not switch systemic immunosuppressive therapy immediately; treat first with topical GCs.
recommendations.context: An isolated, short-lived AAU episode during otherwise well-controlled disease.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Table 2, Education about treatment of AAU

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and CAU controlled on systemic therapy who still use 1-2 drops/day of prednisolone acetate 1% or equivalent, taper topical GCs before tapering systemic therapy.
recommendations.context: Treatment tapering while CAU is controlled but topical GCs remain in use.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Table 2, Taper therapy for uveitis

recommendations.statement: For children and adolescents with JIA and uveitis well controlled using DMARD and biologic systemic therapy only, wait until disease has been well controlled for at least 2 years before tapering therapy.
recommendations.context: Tapering systemic treatment when topical therapy is no longer used.
recommendations.source_heading: RESULTS — Table 2, Taper therapy for uveitis

artifacts.title: Interpretation of strong and conditional recommendations
artifacts.source_heading: RESULTS — How to interpret the recommendations

rows: Patients
Most individuals in this situation would choose the recommended action; only a small minority would decline it.
A majority would choose the suggested action, although many would not. Decision aids can help align choices with individual risks, values, and preferences.
Clinicians
The recommended action is appropriate for most people. Formal decision aids are generally unnecessary for matching decisions to individual values and preferences.

Appropriate choices can differ between patients. Clinicians should help each person make a decision consistent with their values and preferences; decision aids may help account for individual risks, values, and preferences.
Policy makers
The recommendation can generally become policy. Following it may serve as a quality criterion or performance indicator.
Policy decisions require substantial discussion with relevant stakeholders. Performance measures should examine whether the decision-making process is appropriate.
Researchers

Credible research or other persuasive judgments support the recommendation, making it unlikely that additional research will change it. A strong recommendation can nevertheless rest on low or very low certainty of the evidence; in those circumstances, further research may yield important information that changes the recommendation.

Additional research is likely to strengthen the recommendation in later updates or adaptations. Examining the conditions, criteria, judgments, evidence, and other considerations behind its conditional rather than strong status can reveal research gaps.

artifacts.summary: The table explains what strong and conditional recommendations mean for patients, clinicians, policy makers, and researchers.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It helps clinicians apply the stated recommendation strength without treating a conditional choice as appropriate for every patient.

artifacts.title: Recommendations for ophthalmic screening, ophthalmic monitoring, and treatment of children with JIA-associated uveitis, including modifications by the CRA Uveitis Working Group

rows: Ophthalmic screening

For children and adolescents with JIA at high risk of uveitis: conditionally recommend screening at least every 3 months for at least the first 4 years of disease rather than at another frequency. For newly diagnosed, asymptomatic patients, arrange the first examination as early as possible after diagnosis, within the first 1-3 months (adapted).
Ophthalmic monitoring

For children and adolescents with JIA and controlled uveitis: when topical GC is tapered or stopped, strongly recommend an eye examination within 1 month after each change rather than less frequent monitoring (adopted). During stable therapy, strongly recommend examinations no less often than every 3 months (adopted). When systemic therapy is tapered or stopped, strongly recommend examination within 2 months of the change rather than less frequent monitoring (adopted).
GC use

For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU: conditionally recommend PSL acetate 1% eye drops rather than difluprednate eye drops (adopted); for short-term control, conditionally recommend adding or increasing topical GCs rather than adding systemic GCs (adopted). For JIA and CAU requiring > 2 drops/day of PSL acetate 1% to control uveitis: if systemic therapy is not being used, conditionally recommend adding it to permit tapering topical GCs rather than continuing topical GCs alone (adapted). If > 2 drops/day of PSL acetate 1% (or equivalent) remain necessary for at least 3 months despite systemic therapy, conditionally recommend changing or escalating systemic treatment rather than continuing it unchanged (adapted). For new CAU activity during stable systemic therapy, conditionally recommend topical GCs before changing or escalating systemic treatment rather than changing or escalating it immediately (adopted).
DMARDs and biologics

For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU: on starting systemic uveitis treatment, conditionally recommend MTX as the first-line DMARD (developed de novo). When initiating a TNFi, conditionally recommend a monoclonal antibody TNFi rather than ETN (adopted). After an inadequate response to one monoclonal TNFi, conditionally recommend optimizing its dose and/or frequency instead of switching to another monoclonal antibody TNFi (adapted). After failure of a first monoclonal antibody TNFi given at above standard dose and/or frequency, conditionally recommend another monoclonal antibody TNFi rather than a biologic from another class (adopted). After failure of MTX and 2 monoclonal antibody TNFis at optimized dose, conditionally recommend ABA or tocilizumab as biologic DMARD options instead of nonbiologic DMARD options (mycophenolate, leflunomide, cyclosporine) (adapted).
Education about treatment of AAU

For children and adolescents with SpA: strongly recommend education about AAU warning signs to reduce delays in treatment, symptom duration, or uveitis complications (adopted). For those whose disease is well controlled with systemic immunosuppressive therapy (DMARD, biologics) but who develop an isolated, short-lived AAU episode, conditionally recommend against immediately switching systemic immunosuppressive therapy; use topical GCs first (adopted).
Taper therapy for uveitis

For children and adolescents with JIA and CAU controlled by systemic therapy who still use 1-2 drops/day of prednisolone acetate 1% (or equivalent), strongly recommend tapering topical GCs before systemic therapy (adopted). For JIA and uveitis well controlled using only systemic DMARD and biologic therapy, conditionally recommend at least 2 years of well-controlled disease before tapering treatment (adopted).

artifacts.description: The table is adapted from the ACR/AF guidelines; every recommendation has very low quality of evidence. Its high-risk screening group consists of children with oligoarthritis, polyarthritis (rheumatoid factor negative), psoriatic arthritis, or undifferentiated arthritis who are also antinuclear antibody positive, were aged < 7 years at JIA onset, and have JIA duration of ≤ 4 years. New CAU activity means either uveitis not previously present or renewed activity after prior control. The table defines AAU as acute anterior uveitis; ABA as abatacept; ACR as American College of Rheumatology; AF as Arthritis Foundation; CAU as chronic anterior uveitis; CRA as Canadian Rheumatology Association; DMARD as disease-modifying antirheumatic drug; ETN as etanercept; GC as glucocorticoid; JIA as juvenile idiopathic arthritis; MTX as methotrexate; PSL as prednisolone; SpA as spondyloarthritis; and TNFi as tumor necrosis factor inhibitor.
artifacts.summary: The table consolidates screening, monitoring, treatment, education, and tapering recommendations. It identifies recommendations adopted or adapted from the ACR/AF guidelines and the recommendation developed de novo.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: It provides the recommendation strength, patient circumstances, and treatment thresholds needed to choose surveillance intervals and adjust therapy for JIA-associated uveitis.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents at high risk of CAU: those with oligoarthritis, polyarthritis (rheumatoid factor negative), psoriatic arthritis, or undifferentiated arthritis who are antinuclear antibody positive, were aged < 7 years at JIA onset, and have had JIA for ≤ 4 years.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor ophthalmic screening at least every 3 months during at least the first 4 years of disease rather than another screening frequency.
For newly diagnosed patients without symptoms, arrange the first screening examination as soon as possible after diagnosis, within the first 1 to 3 months.

An ophthalmologist is the preferred screening provider. Another eyecare provider may perform timely screening when ophthalmology access is unavailable; an ophthalmologist with uveitis expertise should verify the examination when possible.

recommended_regimens.name: Ophthalmic screening
recommended_regimens.summary: Screen high-risk children and adolescents regularly for ocular inflammation, including an early examination after JIA diagnosis.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At least every 3 months for at least the first 4 years of disease; first examination within the first 1 to 3 months after diagnosis if asymptomatic.

supportive_care: Explain the importance of timely initial and continuing eye examinations to caregivers.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Screening frequency requires communication between rheumatology and ophthalmology. Travel, funding, and limited access to ophthalmologists can impede timely screening, particularly in rural or remote areas.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with controlled uveitis who are tapering or discontinuing topical GC.
decision_rules: Strongly favor ophthalmic assessment within 1 month after each topical GC change rather than less frequent assessment.

recommended_regimens.name: Ophthalmic monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Reassess ocular disease after every reduction or discontinuation of topical GC.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 1 month after each topical GC change.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1 month after each topical GC change

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with controlled uveitis receiving stable therapy.
decision_rules: Strongly favor ophthalmic monitoring no less frequently than every 3 months.

recommended_regimens.name: Ophthalmic monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Continue periodic eye assessments while treatment remains unchanged and uveitis is controlled.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: No less frequently than every 3 months.

response_assessment.timepoint: No less frequently than every 3 months

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with controlled uveitis who are tapering or discontinuing systemic therapy.
decision_rules: Strongly favor an ophthalmic examination within 2 months of a systemic therapy change rather than less frequent monitoring.

recommended_regimens.name: Ophthalmic monitoring
recommended_regimens.summary: Assess ocular disease after reducing or stopping systemic treatment.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Within 2 months of changing systemic therapy.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 2 months of changing systemic therapy

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU requiring topical GC.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor PSL acetate 1% topical drops over difluprednate topical drops.

recommended_regimens.name: PSL acetate 1%
recommended_regimens.summary: Use this topical GC preferentially to difluprednate drops for active CAU.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The preference over difluprednate is conditional, not a prohibition of difluprednate. Prolonged topical GC exposure should be avoided because the document identifies increased intraocular pressure and cataract formation as potential adverse effects.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU needing short-term control.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor adding or increasing topical GCs rather than adding systemic GCs for short-term control.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Add topical GCs or increase their use when short-term control of active CAU is needed, in preference to adding systemic GCs.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: Short-term control; no specific course length stated.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The conditional preference for topical treatment does not constitute an explicit recommendation against systemic GCs.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and CAU who are not receiving systemic therapy and still require more than 2 drops per day of prednisolone acetate 1% (or equivalent) at 3 months after starting uveitis treatment.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor adding systemic therapy to permit topical GC tapering rather than continuing topical GCs alone.
Individualize escalation through shared decision-making. Escalation may also be considered at 1 to 2 drops per day when adherence to drops is poor or their use imposes a substantial burden.

recommended_regimens.name: Systemic therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Add systemic treatment when persistent topical GC requirements exceed the specified threshold, with the aim of reducing topical GC exposure.

response_assessment.timepoint: 3 months after the start of uveitis treatment
response_assessment.method: Assess the daily requirement for prednisolone acetate 1% (or equivalent) topical drops and the need for systemic treatment.
response_assessment.interpretation: A requirement for more than 2 drops per day meets the specified threshold for considering systemic treatment. Steroid-dependent disease apparently controlled at this level is included within active uveitis.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The group associated prolonged use of 3 or more topical GC drops per day with greater risk of ocular complications. The treatment decision remains conditional and individualized.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and CAU who receive systemic treatment for uveitis control but require more than 2 drops per day of prednisolone acetate 1% (or equivalent) for at least 3 months.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor changing or escalating systemic therapy over continuing the existing systemic regimen unchanged.

recommended_regimens.name: Changing or escalating systemic therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Modify systemic treatment when ongoing topical GC dependence exceeds the specified threshold despite systemic therapy.

response_assessment.method: Assess topical GC drop requirements while on systemic treatment.
response_assessment.interpretation: Continued need for more than 2 drops per day meets the stated criterion for changing or escalating systemic therapy; steroid-dependent apparently controlled uveitis counts as active disease.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Escalation should be individualized through shared decision-making; burden or nonadherence associated with drops may justify considering escalation at 1 to 2 drops per day.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA who develop new CAU activity despite stable systemic therapy; new activity includes first-onset uveitis or loss of control of previously controlled uveitis.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor treating first with topical GCs rather than immediately changing or escalating systemic therapy.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat new ocular activity with topical GCs before deciding whether systemic treatment must be altered.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation concerns the initial response to new activity while systemic treatment has remained stable.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and CAU starting systemic treatment for uveitis.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor MTX as the initial DMARD.

Select the initial MTX administration route after considering dose, existing or potential complications, patient and caregiver preferences and comfort with injections, and provincial funding requirements that could affect timely biologic escalation.

recommended_regimens.name: MTX
recommended_regimens.summary: Use MTX as the first-line systemic DMARD. Retrospective studies described safety and efficacy at 15 mg/m2 (alternatively up to 1 mg/kg) to a maximum of 25 mg weekly; the guideline does not present those study doses as a separate graded dosing recommendation.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The working group favored MTX monotherapy over starting dual therapy, but reported no direct evidence comparing the approaches. It removed the source guideline's preference for subcutaneous over oral MTX because high-quality evidence of clinical superiority in JIA-associated uveitis was lacking. mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), azathioprine, and cyclosporine were described as having variable success and being tried most often after MTX-refractory disease, rather than as equally recommended initial options.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU starting a TNFi.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor starting a monoclonal antibody TNFi rather than ETN.

recommended_regimens.name: monoclonal antibody TNFi
recommended_regimens.summary: Choose a monoclonal antibody TNFi when TNFi treatment is initiated for active CAU, in preference to ETN.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The conditional comparison with ETN is not an explicit prohibition of ETN.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU with an inadequate response to one monoclonal antibody TNFi at standard JIA dosing.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor optimizing the dose and/or frequency of the current monoclonal antibody TNFi instead of switching immediately to another monoclonal antibody TNFi.

For adalimumab (ADA), the document identifies product-monograph dosing of 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks for patients weighing more than 30 kg and discusses treatment with 40 mg subcutaneously weekly to seek maximal clinical benefit.
For infliximab, shortening the interval to less than every 4 weeks and/or increasing the dose to more than 10 mg/kg may be considered.

recommended_regimens.name: Optimization of the current monoclonal antibody TNFi
recommended_regimens.summary: Adjust the existing monoclonal antibody TNFi dose and/or administration frequency following an inadequate response at standard JIA dosing.

response_assessment.method: Assess response to the current monoclonal antibody TNFi at standard JIA dosing.
response_assessment.interpretation: An inadequate response prompts consideration of dose and/or frequency optimization before switching.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document reports no randomized controlled comparison between monoclonal TNFis for JIA-associated CAU. It states that weekly adalimumab (ADA) at the discussed dose has not been accompanied by a significant increase in reported adverse effects; older case series are cited in support of infliximab optimization safety. Access and reimbursement for dosing beyond standard schedules may vary.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU after failure of a first monoclonal antibody TNFi at above standard dose and/or frequency.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor changing to another monoclonal antibody TNFi over changing to a biologic in a different class.

recommended_regimens.name: Another monoclonal antibody TNFi
recommended_regimens.summary: Switch within the monoclonal antibody TNFi group after failure of the first such treatment at above standard dose and/or frequency.

response_assessment.timepoint: After treatment at above standard dose and/or frequency
response_assessment.method: Assess response to the first monoclonal antibody TNFi.
response_assessment.interpretation: Failure at this stage supports a conditional preference for another monoclonal antibody TNFi over a biologic from a different class.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The comparative recommendation does not explicitly prohibit use of a biologic from another class.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU after failure of MTX and 2 monoclonal antibody TNFis at optimized doses.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor abatacept (ABA) or tocilizumab (TCZ) as biologic DMARD options over the nonbiologic DMARD options MMF, leflunomide, or cyclosporine.

recommended_regimens.name: abatacept (ABA)
recommended_regimens.summary: A biologic DMARD option conditionally favored over the specified nonbiologic DMARDs for refractory CAU.

recommended_regimens.name: tocilizumab (TCZ)
recommended_regimens.summary: A biologic DMARD option conditionally favored over the specified nonbiologic DMARDs for refractory CAU.

response_assessment.timepoint: After failure of MTX and 2 monoclonal antibody TNFis at optimized doses
response_assessment.interpretation: Failure of these treatments defines the population for whom the biologic DMARD preference applies.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document states that evidence does not guide treatment after failure of 2 monoclonal TNFis; this conditional preference reflects expert opinion informed by observational data. It also discusses daclizumab, rituximab, and golimumab as investigated agents, without recommending them as equivalent options in this pathway. For loss of efficacy over time, the cited SHARE group suggests considering antidrug antibody and drug trough-level testing; if antibodies are absent but trough levels are low, a dose increase or shorter interval may be an option. The document reports no direct evidence on these measurements' effects on biologic clinical efficacy in uveitis.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with SpA who need to recognize possible AAU.
decision_rules: Strongly favor education about AAU warning signs to reduce delays in treatment, symptom duration, or uveitis complications.

recommended_regimens.name: Education about AAU warning signs
recommended_regimens.summary: Teach patients to recognize warning signs of AAU so that care is not delayed.

supportive_care: Provide education on AAU warning signs.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The document does not enumerate the individual warning signs.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with SpA whose disease is well controlled with systemic immunosuppressive therapy (DMARD, biologics) and who develop an isolated, short-lived AAU episode.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor topical GCs first rather than immediately switching systemic immunosuppressive therapy.

recommended_regimens.name: Topical GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat the isolated, short-lived AAU episode locally before changing an otherwise effective systemic regimen.

not_recommended.name: Immediate switch of systemic immunosuppressive therapy
not_recommended.reason: The guideline conditionally recommends against an immediate switch for an isolated, short-lived AAU episode while systemic treatment is providing good control, favoring topical GCs first.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The recommendation against switching applies to an immediate switch in this specific setting, not to every subsequent systemic treatment change.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA whose CAU is controlled on systemic therapy but who remain on 1-2 drops/day of prednisolone acetate 1% (or equivalent).
decision_rules: Strongly favor tapering topical GCs before tapering systemic therapy.

recommended_regimens.name: Tapering topical GCs
recommended_regimens.summary: Reduce topical GC treatment first while CAU remains controlled on systemic treatment.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 1 month after each topical GC change

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The guideline strongly recommends the tapering order; it does not prohibit later tapering of systemic therapy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Children and adolescents with JIA and uveitis that is well controlled using DMARD and biologic systemic therapy only.
decision_rules: Conditionally favor waiting until disease has been well controlled for at least 2 years before tapering systemic therapy.

recommended_regimens.name: Tapering systemic therapy
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider reducing systemic therapy only after the specified period of sustained uveitis control.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: At least 2 years of well-controlled disease before tapering.

response_assessment.timepoint: At least 2 years of well-controlled disease
response_assessment.method: Assess sustained uveitis control before beginning systemic treatment taper.
response_assessment.interpretation: This is the conditionally recommended minimum period of control before tapering.

response_assessment.timepoint: Within 2 months of changing systemic therapy

document_sections.heading: ABSTRACT.
document_sections.content: Objective: Develop Canadian guidance for screening, monitoring, and treating uveitis associated with juvenile idiopathic arthritis (JIA). Methods: Recommendations were developed through GRADE-ADOLOPMENT. A group of 14 pediatric rheumatologists, 6 ophthalmologists, 2 methodologists, and 3 caregiver/patient representatives reviewed recent American College of Rheumatology (ACR)/Arthritis Foundation (AF) guidance. Members prepared evidence-to-decision (EtD) tables in pairs, surveyed agreement, and discussed and voted on selected recommendations at a virtual meeting. Health equity was considered throughout. Results: A survey identified 7 of 19 recommendations for detailed discussion. Seventy-five percent of members attended the virtual meeting, which addressed the first eye examination, screening intervals, escalation of systemic and biologic treatment, and nonbiologic treatment. Differences in access to care and advanced therapies across Canadian provinces and territories were highlighted. Subsequently, 5 recommendations were adapted, 2 were removed, and 1 was created de novo. Conclusion: The resulting guidance reflects the Canadian context, including cost, equity, and access, and incorporates pediatric rheumatology, uveitis ophthalmology, and parent/patient perspectives.

document_sections.heading: Canadian Rheumatology Association Recommendations for the Screening, Monitoring, and Treatment of Juvenile Idiopathic Arthritis-Associated Uveitis
document_sections.content: Chronic anterior uveitis can be asymptomatic, affects up to 20% of children with JIA, and can cause substantial morbidity, including permanent vision loss. Regular eye examinations that detect inflammation early, followed by prompt appropriate treatment, can preserve good vision and prevent complications. Female sex, JIA onset at age < 7, and antinuclear antibody (ANA) positivity are risk factors. The reported cumulative incidence of new uveitis during the first 5 years after JIA diagnosis was 13.9%, supporting careful screening during that period. Care requires cooperation between rheumatology and ophthalmology; other eye care providers may sometimes participate in screening. Management may involve topical and/or systemic therapies, frequent visits, and treatment changes. The ACR/AF published North American guidance in 2019 addressing screening, monitoring, and treatment, including systemic immunosuppression for uveitis dependent on or refractory to topical glucocorticoids (GCs). Prolonged topical GC treatment should be avoided because it can increase intraocular pressure and cause cataracts. Only 3 published controlled trials specifically evaluated systemic treatment for JIA-associated uveitis, leaving limited evidence and making regulatory approval difficult. Canadian access to specialist care and biologics differs by province, creating a need for nationally applicable guidance. The ACR/AF guidance was selected as a starting point because it used GRADE methodology and addressed all 3 aspects of care. GRADE-ADOLOPMENT was used to examine Canadian preferences, resources, costs, and implementation feasibility without duplicating prior work. EtD tables supported transparent judgments before recommendations were adopted, adapted, or developed de novo. Adoption retains a trustworthy existing recommendation; adaptation appraises relevant existing guidance and determines whether to retain or change it; de novo development answers a question absent from the source guidance. This is the first Canadian guidance on JIA-associated uveitis and the first Canadian Rheumatology Association (CRA) guideline to use GRADE-ADOLOPMENT.

document_sections.heading: METHODS
document_sections.content: The working group included 14 pediatric rheumatologists representing 13 of 14 Canadian academic centers, plus 1 community-based pediatric rheumatologist and 1 trainee; 6 geographically diverse ophthalmologists with uveitis expertise or subspecialty training; and 3 parent/patient champions. The CRA guidelines committee chair, a Cochrane Musculoskeletal representative, and a research associate participated without voting. Members completed conflict-of-interest forms before the project. An updated systematic search using the ACR/AF search terms covered OVID MEDLINE, Embase, PubMed, and the Cochrane Library from October 13, 2017 to February 6, 2020. Separate reviews addressed equity, patient preferences, and economics. For each article, 2 members extracted data and prepared summary-of-finding (SoF) tables. Evidence quality was rated high, moderate, low, or very low after considering bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision, and other GRADE factors. Pairs of 2 members reviewed each source recommendation, its PICO question, selected studies, and SoF tables. Pairing reflected the clinical question and geographic diversity. An equity filter considered Indigenous populations, rural/remote residence, refugee status, and low socioeconomic status/homelessness. Each pair prepared an EtD table covering benefits, harms, baseline risk, patient values, resource use, costs, feasibility, acceptability, and possible effects on health equity. RB and DML reviewed the tables with input from GSH and JPP, after which pairs revised them. All members completed an online survey about adopting each recommendation unchanged or with revised wording, additional Canadian considerations, and the need for meeting discussion. Recommendations for which > 50% of respondents sought disagreement/discussion were brought to a virtual meeting. The meeting took place in August 2020; an in-person meeting was not possible because of coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19). Nonvoting advisors facilitated presentation, discussion, and voting on the recommendations. The prespecified consensus threshold was 80% of voting members; agreement on every adapted and newly created recommendation reached 100%. Research Ethics Board approval was not required.

document_sections.heading: RESULTS
document_sections.content: After duplicate removal, searches yielded 410 citations about JIA-associated uveitis and 554 articles about equity, preferences, and economics. Articles were reviewed and graded against the source guideline’s 19 PICO questions. DP and HYN screened independently, with RB or DML resolving disagreements. Another 22 articles were identified. The review produced SoF tables (n = 26) for observational studies, GRADE tables (n = 2) for trials, and updates to the ACR tables. Evidence was low quality for every PICO question, mainly because evidence was scarce and indirect; most studies were observational, a design considered low quality in GRADE. Rural and remote implementation, Indigenous populations, low socioeconomic status, and treatment access informed every recommendation. The CRA guidance retained the ACR/AF definitions, treatment interventions, and critical or important outcomes. The figure depicts the searches used to identify relevant articles. The survey supported adopting 13 source recommendations as presented. The remaining 6 were discussed at a meeting attended by 75% (15/20) of the working group, 3 parent/patient representatives, and 2 nonvoting advisors. The document also identifies 7 recommendations needing substantial revision: screening (n = 1) and treatment (n = 6). Ultimately, 5 source recommendations were adapted (ACR/AF recommendations 1, 8, 9, 13, and 15), 2 were removed (ACR/AF recommendations 10 and 11), and 1 was developed de novo (new recommendation 4). Comments from absent members were incorporated, and discussion achieved 100% consensus on the 7 recommendations. Table 2 brings together screening, monitoring, treatment, education, and tapering recommendations; each has very low quality of evidence. Its adopted recommendations strongly favor ophthalmic review within 1 month after each topical GC reduction or discontinuation, at least every 3 months during stable treatment, and within 2 months after a change made to taper or stop systemic therapy, for children and adolescents with JIA and controlled uveitis. For active CAU, it conditionally favors PSL acetate 1% drops over difluprednate drops, and short-term addition or increase of topical GCs over systemic GCs. When new CAU activity occurs despite stable systemic treatment, it conditionally favors topical GCs before an immediate systemic change; new activity means either first uveitis or renewed activity after previous control. For active CAU requiring a TNFi, it conditionally favors starting a monoclonal antibody TNFi over ETN. After failure of a first monoclonal antibody TNFi at above standard dose and/or frequency, it conditionally favors another monoclonal antibody TNFi over a biologic from another class. For children and adolescents with SpA, education about AAU warning signs is strongly recommended to reduce treatment delay, symptom duration, or complications. If systemic immunosuppression controls disease but an isolated, short-lived AAU episode develops, the guidance conditionally recommends against immediately switching systemic treatment in favor of trying topical GCs first. For CAU controlled with systemic treatment while 1-2 drops/day of prednisolone acetate 1% or equivalent continue, tapering topical GCs before systemic treatment is strongly recommended. When uveitis is well controlled using DMARD and biologic systemic treatment alone, the guidance conditionally recommends at least 2 years of disease control before tapering.

document_sections.heading: How to interpret the recommendations.
document_sections.content: Recommendation strength is expressed as strong or conditional. Table 1 explains the implications for patients, clinicians, policy makers, and researchers. With a strong recommendation, most patients would choose the recommended course, clinicians should generally follow it, and policy adoption is usually possible. With a conditional recommendation, the majority would choose the suggested course but many would not; individual values and circumstances therefore matter, and policy decisions require wider deliberation. Decision aids may help with conditional choices. A strong recommendation may occasionally rest on low or very low certainty evidence, in which case further research could change it. Research may also clarify the factors underlying a conditional recommendation.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 1 (ACR/AF recommendation 1 adapted).
document_sections.content: For children and adolescents with JIA at high risk of CAU, screening at least every 3 months during the first 4 years is conditionally recommended rather than a different interval. Newly diagnosed, asymptomatic patients should have an initial eye assessment as soon as possible, within the first 1 to 3 months (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Rheumatologists and ophthalmologists should communicate closely when selecting screening frequency. The minimum frequency allows closer assessment when vision is threatened. Relevant risk factors include JIA onset at < 7 years, oligoarticular subtype, female sex, and ANA positivity. Table 2 defines its high-risk group as children with oligoarthritis, polyarthritis (rheumatoid factor negative), psoriatic arthritis, or undifferentiated arthritis who are also ANA positive, were aged < 7 years at JIA onset, and have JIA duration of ≤ 4 years. Caregivers need to understand the timing because asymptomatic disease can otherwise delay diagnosis. Expert discussion supported an initial examination within 1 to 3 months regardless of location, while recognizing travel and funding barriers in rural/remote areas. An ophthalmologist is the preferred screening provider; another eye care provider may screen when timely ophthalmology access is unavailable. An ophthalmologist experienced in uveitis should verify the examination when feasible.

document_sections.heading: Recommendations 2 and 3 (ACR/AF recommendation 8 and 9 adapted).
document_sections.content: Recommendation 2: For children and adolescents with JIA and CAU who still need more than 2 drops per day of prednisolone acetate 1% or equivalent at 3 months after uveitis treatment begins and are not receiving systemic treatment, adding systemic treatment to permit topical GC tapering is conditionally recommended rather than continuing topical GCs alone (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). Recommendation 3: If more than 2 drops per day remain necessary for at least 3 months despite systemic treatment for uveitis, changing or escalating systemic treatment is conditionally recommended rather than leaving it unchanged (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). The ACR/AF source used a threshold of 1 to 2 drops per day. Published evidence associates more than 2 daily topical GC drops with ocular complications; the group considered long-term use of 3 or more drops per day to increase this risk, while acknowledging limited evidence. Australia- and New Zealand–based expert consensus guidance also supports a threshold greater than 2 drops per day. Escalation should be individualized through shared decision-making. With nonadherence or substantial treatment burden, it may be considered even when 1 to 2 drops per day are needed. The group agreed on a maximum 3-month monitoring interval before considering systemic treatment. Its interpretation of active uveitis includes steroid-dependent disease that appears controlled only while more than 2 topical steroid drops are used daily.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 4 (developed de novo).
document_sections.content: For children and adolescents with JIA and CAU starting systemic CAU treatment, methotrexate (MTX) is conditionally recommended as the first-line disease-modifying antirheumatic drug (DMARD; conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). The ACR/AF guidance did not explicitly select an initial systemic drug, whereas SHARE and Australia/New Zealand consensus guidance supports MTX first. Retrospective studies report safety and efficacy for JIA-associated uveitis at 15 mg/m2, alternatively up to 1 mg/kg, to a maximum of 25 mg weekly; subsequent systematic reviews confirmed those findings. Other consensus guidelines likewise favor MTX first. mycophenolate mofetil (MMF), azathioprine, and cyclosporine have been used with variable success, usually after MTX failure, but their studies contain very small patient numbers. Evidence for MTX is more robust than for these other conventional DMARDs despite generally limited study quality. The source guidance conditionally preferred subcutaneous to oral MTX, citing bioavailability data at doses greater than 15 mg/m2; other cited consensus plans agreed. However, high-quality evidence of superior clinical outcomes with subcutaneous MTX in JIA-associated uveitis is lacking, so that route recommendation was removed. Initial route selection should account for dose, actual or potential complications, caregiver/patient preferences and comfort with injections, and provincial funding rules after MTX failure so escalation is not delayed. The source also conditionally preferred starting dual therapy rather than MTX alone; the Canadian group instead favored MTX monotherapy and removed the source recommendation. There is no direct evidence comparing these approaches or comparing their complication and safety risks. Access to first-line tumor necrosis factor inhibitors (TNFis) in Canada was another concern. Ophthalmologists reported no standardized definition of severe or sight-threatening complications. The ACR/AF source defined severe disease by structural ocular complications of uveitis or complications from topical steroids. Severity need not imply greater treatment difficulty because it differs from chronicity. Posterior synechiae and cataracts indicate poorer visual outcomes, but the group removed the term severe.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 5 (ACR/AF recommendation 13 adapted).
document_sections.content: For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU responding inadequately to one monoclonal antibody TNFi at standard JIA dosing, optimizing that drug’s dose and/or frequency is conditionally recommended instead of switching immediately to another monoclonal antibody TNFi (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). No randomized controlled trial directly compares monoclonal TNFis for this indication. The group considered access inequities associated with the source wording above standard dosing, which could depend on the treatment site or reimbursement. The adalimumab (ADA) product monograph gives 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks for patients weighing more than 30 kg. Treatment with 40 mg subcutaneously weekly may yield maximal clinical benefit, with no significant increase in reported adverse effects. For infliximab, an interval of less than every 4 weeks and/or a dose of more than 10 mg/kg may be considered; older case series support its safety. Patient/caregiver advisors preferred adjusting an existing regimen to introducing a different drug unless a clear benefit justified the change.

document_sections.heading: Recommendation 6 (ACR/AF recommendation 15 adapted).
document_sections.content: For children and adolescents with JIA and active CAU who have failed MTX and 2 monoclonal antibody TNFis at optimized doses, abatacept (ABA) or tocilizumab (TCZ) are conditionally recommended as biologic DMARD (bDMARD) options rather than nonbiologic DMARD (nbDMARD) options comprising MMF, leflunomide, or cyclosporine (conditional recommendation, very low certainty of evidence). No evidence directly guides CAU treatment after failure of 2 monoclonal TNFis. The ACR/AF source expressed no preference between bDMARD and nbDMARD options; the Canadian preference reflects expert judgment and observational data. Investigated biologics also include daclizumab, rituximab, and the alternative monoclonal TNFi golimumab. Studied biologic treatments show some benefit in patients refractory to conventional treatment. In monoclonal TNFi–refractory uveitis, the reviewed literature offers no direct evidence linking low trough concentrations or antidrug antibodies to clinical efficacy. SHARE, drawing on other clinical settings, advises considering antibody and trough-level tests when efficacy wanes over time. If antibodies are absent but trough levels are low, increasing the dose or shortening the dosing interval may be an option.

document_sections.heading: DISCUSSION
document_sections.content: Canadian adaptations concern the first screening examination, the topical GC threshold for systemic escalation (> 2 drops/day of prednisolone acetate 1% for > 3 months), a step-up approach beginning with conditionally recommended MTX, removal of the subcutaneous-versus-oral MTX preference because of insufficient evidence, optimization rather than automatic switching of a TNFi, and preference for biologic over nonbiologic treatment after MTX and TNFi failure. First-line biologic access and limited evidence influenced the step-up approach. The 2019 ACR/AF guidance covered GC, nbDMARD, and bDMARD treatment for CAU, alongside screening, monitoring, and education and care for AAU risk or disease. It used GRADE and involved pediatric rheumatologists, ophthalmologists, adult patients with JIA, and a separate caregiver/patient panel. Its overall evidence quality was very low and most recommendations were conditional, but it addressed an important clinical gap. GRADE-ADOLOPMENT was chosen because the source guidance was recent and rigorous and the countries share access challenges. Canadian differences include 10 provincially and 3 territorially regulated public and private medication payment models, while the Non-Insured Health Benefits program provides federally regulated coverage for First Nations and Inuit populations. Access to pediatric rheumatology and ophthalmology expertise varies geographically: Canada has approximately 1 rheumatologist per 75,000 children and only 3 ophthalmologists per 100,000 population, with fewer specialists experienced in pediatric uveitis. Specialists are concentrated in certain cities, and some remote patients travel more than 2000 km to a treating center. Other eye care providers may therefore need to assist with screening. Updated systematic evidence and EtD tables made the recommendation process more transparent and efficient. Canada lacks national pharmacare; provincial biologic access varies, and off-label use can be difficult because of cost and limited compassionate supply. Biosimilars may improve equitable access. As of May 2021, 4 new ADA biosimilars had Health Canada indications for pediatric uveitis. Availability and coverage vary, some private plans follow public reimbursement standards, and over the past 2 years some provinces have adopted nonmedical switching from originator biologics to biosimilars to save healthcare funds. The working group completed the adaptation in less than 1 year of effective work at low cost and incorporated updated evidence. Most source recommendations were adopted with minor changes because Canadian judgments generally did not substantially alter their direction or strength. The authors recommend GRADE-ADOLOPMENT when trustworthy, transparently developed source guidance and supporting materials exist. The resulting recommendations aim to support coordinated uveitis care and more equitable Canadian access.
